Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Vikram had been forty-two when the borders closed, his neighborhood swept up in a sudden collapse that turned familiar streets into a maze of collapsing checkpoints and running crowds. He remembered the heat of the dust, the sharp cracks of gunfire, and the heavy thud of a wounded boy sliding past his boots. He had held the boy's hand until the medics pulled him away, yet he had stayed behind, certain that moving meant leaving him to the same fate. He told himself he had been protecting the rest of the convoy, but the thought that he had not done enough never left him. He felt guilty for surviving when others did not, watching the rest of his family cross while he remained in the smoke. The memory of that day surfaces not as a story he can tell, but as a sudden pressure in his chest, a flash of soot and steel that refuses to be put into words. Sometimes he watches the event unfold in his mind with complete detachment, as if observing a stranger's misfortune, but other times the quiet recollection fractures into an overwhelming grief that leaves him sitting at his kitchen table long after the coffee has gone cold. He had come to believe that he had permanently changed for the worse, that the man who once moved through crowds without hesitation was now a person who measured every distance. In the weeks that followed his resettlement, the quiet of everyday life began to feel dangerously exposed. His body learned to stay on guard, and he found himself scanning doorways and windows before allowing himself to relax. He always identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, counting exits and mapping a path back to the street. He avoided large open spaces, where the lack of walls made him feel as though he had nowhere to retreat if the ground gave way again. He also steered clear of police officers and military personnel, not because he disliked them, but because the sight of their uniforms and the glint of their sidearms felt like a sudden return to the checkpoints. When authority figures approached or questions came quickly, his instinct was to yield, to smile, to agree, to keep the peace even when his shoulders tightened with unspoken tension. These patterns sat side by side with his daily rhythm; he did not feel driven by one, but rather carried them all forward, adjusting his steps to the weight of each. His work as a chef at a bustling downtown restaurant became the specific stage where his triggers took root. The open kitchen, with its stainless steel counters and constant flow of staff, mirrored the exposed spaces he avoided elsewhere. He positioned himself near the back doors during shifts, his eyes tracking the street where ambulances sometimes wailed past on their way to the hospital. The sound of those sirens made his stomach tighten, not with panic, but with a sharp, familiar alertness. He started listening closely when his coworkers discussed a recent car crash near the market or the kitchen equipment failure that had sent a prep cook to urgent care; crash discussions pulled his attention instantly. He watched his staff closely, noticing the redness of a sprained ankle, the bandages on a cook's forearm, the way a drop of blood could well up on a cut knuckle. Visual injuries on others mirrored the wounds he had seen at the border, pulling his focus away from the pass. During dinner service, the concentration he needed to time sauces and plates grew fragile; he would lose his place in a recipe, drop a tray, or find himself staring at the kitchen door as if waiting for an order he could not quite hear. Over the months, his avoidance and compliance began to shape his work life in concrete ways. He started declining the larger banquet setups where he would be stranded on the far side of the ballroom, and he took on the quieter, more enclosed prep station. His tendency to fawn meant he accepted extra shifts and extra requests without complaint, even as the accumulated fatigue settled into his posture. He had come to believe that the world remained inherently unstable, and his colleagues noticed the quiet shift, the way he would nod along to a manager's instructions even when the pacing grew frantic. What finally brought him to seek help was not a crisis, but a quiet accumulation: the day an ambulance stopped right outside the restaurant, the sound of the doors closing echoed through the dining room, and he found himself unable to move past the stainless steel pass, certain that if he stepped forward, he would be pulled back into the dust. He went to the clinic hoping, though he was not certain, to learn how to live with the memories without being ruled by them.
